items.explanation: The review says the factory jobs lost were replaced by service work in retail, finance, and health care.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — globalization replaced 'factory jobs with service work in retail, finance, and health care'

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review describes a move into services, not into mining, farming, or fishing.
option_explanations.B: Correct. These are the three service sectors the review names.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Steel, autos, and electronics are the manufacturing industries undercut by foreign competition — the jobs being lost, not the replacements.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The review names retail, finance, and health care, not defense manufacturing.

options: (A) Mining, farming, and fishing.
(B) Retail, finance, and health care.
(C) Steel, autos, and electronics.
(D) Defense manufacturing and shipbuilding.
items.stem: As factory jobs disappeared, which sectors does the review name as absorbing workers into service work?

items.explanation: The review is explicit: the service work that replaced factory jobs meant lower wages, fewer benefits, and less security.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — replacing factory jobs with service work meant 'lower wages, fewer benefits, less security'

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review says the replacement jobs paid less and offered less, not more.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The review contrasts the two: the new service jobs were worse on pay, benefits, and security.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The review ties union decline to the same era; it does not describe service jobs as more unionized.
option_explanations.D: Correct. This is the review's three-part description of the replacement jobs.

options: (A) The service jobs paid more and offered stronger benefits than factory work.
(B) The two kinds of jobs were broadly equivalent in pay, benefits, and security.
(C) The service jobs were more heavily unionized than the factory jobs had been.
(D) The service jobs meant lower wages, fewer benefits, and less security.
items.stem: How does the review characterize the service jobs that replaced factory work, compared with the factory jobs workers lost?

items.explanation: The review names the hollowing out of the Democratic Party's union base as one of deindustrialization's political consequences.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — deindustrialization 'hollowed out the Democratic Party's union base'

option_explanations.A: Correct. As union membership declined, the Democrats' union base hollowed out.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The review says the base was hollowed out, not expanded into the Sun Belt.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The review treats deindustrialization as the economic engine under the period's politics.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The review says nothing about a shift from cities to farms.

options: (A) It hollowed out the party's union base as union membership declined.
(B) It expanded the party's union base into the fast-growing Sun Belt states.
(C) It had no meaningful effect on either party's political base.
(D) It shifted the party's base from the cities out to the farms.
items.stem: According to the review, what did deindustrialization do to the Democratic Party's political base?

items.explanation: The review says the PATCO firing signaled that the new administration would not protect organized labor — a landmark defeat in the union decline it describes.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — 'the PATCO firing (1981) signaled that the new administration wouldn't protect it' (union membership)

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review says the signal was the opposite: the administration would not protect unions.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Firing the striking controllers was not a routine negotiated settlement.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The firing marked a defeat for labor, not a restoration of its power.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The review presents the firing as the signal that the new administration would not protect organized labor.

options: (A) That the administration would expand federal protection for striking workers.
(B) That the strike had been settled through routine negotiation.
(C) That organized labor's power would be restored to its 1950s peak.
(D) That the new administration would not protect organized labor.
items.stem: The review notes Reagan's firing of the striking PATCO air-traffic controllers in 1981. What signal did the review say that action sent?

items.explanation: The review's closing sentence on the topic traces three things to deindustrialization: the hollowing out of the Democratic union base, the resentment behind Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts, and the Sun Belt's rise as the political center of gravity.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — deindustrialization 'hollowed out the Democratic Party's union base, fed the resentment that powered Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts, and explains why the Sun Belt — not the old industrial core — became America's political center of gravity'

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review says regional costs were concentrated and political conflict intensified — the reverse.
option_explanations.B: Correct. These are the political consequences the review traces to deindustrialization.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The review describes backlash and resentment over trade, not consensus.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Both parties continued; the review describes shifts within the party system, not its disappearance.

options: (A) The end of all regional economic differences across the country and a broad, lasting decline in political conflict.
(B) Resentment behind Reagan's 1980 win and later populist revolts, with political gravity shifting to the Sun Belt.
(C) A bipartisan consensus that ended debate over trade and globalization policy for a generation.
(D) The disappearance of the Democratic and Republican parties as national organizations.
items.stem: The review calls deindustrialization “the economic engine under the period's politics.” Which political consequences does it trace to deindustrialization?

items.explanation: The review distinguishes output from employment: manufacturing output stayed high thanks to productivity gains, while manufacturing's share of employment fell. Deindustrialization was a change in the structure of employment, not the end of American production.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — 'Manufacturing output stayed high thanks to productivity gains, but manufacturing's share of American employment fell steadily'

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review says output stayed high — factories did not all close.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The review says output stayed high thanks to productivity gains.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Output held up through productivity even as the employment share declined.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The review describes a large manufacturing sector shrinking as a share of employment, not one that never existed.

options: (A) The review says every American factory had closed its doors by the year 2010.
(B) The review says American manufacturing output fell all the way to zero in those decades.
(C) The review says output stayed high on productivity gains as manufacturing's job share fell.
(D) The review says the United States never had a manufacturing sector in the first place.
items.stem: A student claims that deindustrialization means the United States stopped producing manufactured goods. Which evidence from the review best corrects that claim?

items.explanation: The review's figures describe the bargain at its height: manufacturing at roughly a quarter of jobs around 1970 and union membership at roughly a third of workers in the 1950s. The 1970s broke that arrangement.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — the 1970s 'broke the postwar industrial bargain'; at its height manufacturing held roughly a quarter of jobs (around 1970) and unions covered roughly a third of workers (1950s) (approximate)

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review describes an economy built on factories and unions, not one without them.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The review describes private-sector industrial employment and union coverage, not guaranteed government jobs.
option_explanations.C: Correct. These are the review's own figures for the industrial economy at its height.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The review's story is about manufacturing, not agriculture.

options: (A) An economy with no factories and no unions anywhere in the country at all.
(B) An economy where the federal government guaranteed every single worker a permanent job.
(C) An economy with a quarter of jobs in manufacturing and a third of workers in unions.
(D) An economy where agriculture employed most American workers by a wide margin.
items.stem: The review says the 1970s “broke the postwar industrial bargain.” Drawing only on the figures the review gives, what did that bargain look like at its height?

items.explanation: The review's divergence is geographic: factory closures concentrated in the Northeast and Midwest while people, plants, and political weight shifted to the Sun Belt.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — factories closed across the Northeast and Midwest (the Rust Belt) while the Sun Belt's 'defense industries, lower taxes, and air-conditioned suburbs attracted both people and plants,' and the Sun Belt 'became America's political center of gravity'

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review describes the two regions moving in opposite directions.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The review says the Sun Belt gained — including through defense industries — while the Rust Belt lost factories.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The review's point is the contrast between the declining industrial core and the growing Sun Belt.
option_explanations.D: Correct. This captures the review's Rust Belt–Sun Belt divergence.

options: (A) Both regions lost factories at the same rate and for the same underlying reasons.
(B) The Sun Belt lost its defense industries while the Rust Belt gained new factories instead.
(C) The two regions were economically identical to each other throughout the period.
(D) The Northeast and Midwest lost factories and jobs; the Sun Belt gained people and plants.
items.stem: Which comparison best captures the Rust Belt–Sun Belt divergence the review describes?
